name: docx
tagline: Create, edit, and analyze Word .docx files with full formatting control
triggers: mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', or '.docx'
requests for report, memo, letter, or template as a Word file
working with tracked changes, comments, or headings in a document
extracting or reorganizing content from .docx files
deep_dive: New documents are generated via the `docx` npm library (JavaScript), using Document/Packer/Paragraph/Table/ImageRun and related classes, then validated with a Python `scripts/office/validate.py` script. Existing documents are edited through an unpack-edit-repack cycle: `scripts/office/unpack.py` extracts the ZIP into pretty-printed XML, edits are made directly to the XML using the Edit tool, and `scripts/office/pack.py` repacks with auto-repair. Text extraction uses `pandoc`, legacy .doc conversion uses LibreOffice via `scripts/office/soffice.py`, and PDF/image rendering uses LibreOffice plus Poppler's `pdftoppm`. The skill handles tracked changes, comments (via `scripts/comment.py`), tables of contents, headers/footers, multi-column layouts, footnotes, hyperlinks, and images in both creation and editing paths.
use_when: Producing a polished Word document (report, memo, contract, letter)
Editing an existing .docx file, adding tracked changes or comments
Extracting text or tables from a Word document
Converting a .doc file to .docx before editing
not_for: PDFs (use the pdf skill)
Spreadsheets or Google Docs
General coding tasks unrelated to document generation
overlaps_with: pdf / pptx / xlsx (different file formats — pick by output type)
google-docs (cloud-based Google document instead of a local .docx file)

The `--list` flag enumerates configured databases, `--tables` and `--schema` support schema exploration, and `--limit` applies a row cap. Database auto-selection matches the user's intent keywords against each connection's `description` field.

Exploring the schema or table structure of a Postgres database
Running ad-hoc SELECT queries for data investigation

not_for: Write operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP) — these are blocked by design
MySQL or SQL Server databases (use the mysql or mssql skills)

Workflow: (1) list available subtitles with `--list-subs`; (2) try manual subtitles (`--write-sub --skip-download`) for highest quality; (3) fall back to auto-generated (`--write-auto-sub`); (4) last resort — ask user confirmation, then download audio with `-x --audio-format mp3` and transcribe with `openai-whisper` using the `base` model. Downloaded subtitles are in WebVTT (`.vtt`) format. Post-processing deduplicates overlapping auto-generated caption lines via a Python one-liner that strips VTT headers, timestamps, and HTML tags, writing a clean `.txt` file named after the video title. Temporary VTT and audio files are cleaned up after conversion.

Getting subtitles or captions from a YouTube URL

Saving a cleaned plain-text transcript to a local file

deep_dive: SkillCheck reads the target SKILL.md using only the Read and Glob tools, then applies a layered set of free-tier validation rules in four phases: Parse (extract YAML frontmatter), Validate (run all checks), Score (0-100), and Report. deep_dive: Skill-creator guides the user through a full skill development lifecycle. After the user submits feedback, Claude improves the skill and iterates. For description optimization, it generates 20 trigger/non-trigger eval queries, opens a browser review UI, then runs `scripts/run_loop.py` (up to 5 iterations, 60/40 train/test split) to find the description with the best held-out test score.

deep_dive: The skill operates in three modes: rewrite (audit + full rewrite + diff summary + second-pass audit), detect (flag only, grouped by P0/P1/P2 severity), and edit (minimal in-place file edits using the Edit tool, leaving already-human passages untouched). It applies a tiered vocabulary system: Tier 1 words (always replace, e.g. 'delve', 'leverage', 'robust'), Tier 2 words (flag when 2+ appear in the same paragraph), and Tier 3 words/phrases (flag only at high density). Beyond vocabulary, it checks 40+ structural and stylometric patterns including em-dash frequency, synonym cycling, formulaic closers, hedge-stacked predictions, chatbot artifacts, unfilled placeholders, citation markup leaks, AI-tool URL parameters, rhythm uniformity (sentence/paragraph length), and type-token ratio. Six context profiles (linkedin, blog, technical-blog, investor-email, docs, casual) and five voice profiles (casual, professional, technical, warm, blunt) adjust rule strictness and target register independently.

name: debugging-code
tagline: Interactive DAP-based debugger: set breakpoints, step through code, inspect live state
triggers: program crashes or raises unexpected exceptions
produces wrong output and print-statement debugging isn't enough
need to understand how execution reached a certain state
interactively debug / set breakpoints
deep_dive: The skill uses `dap`, a CLI tool backed by a background daemon that speaks the Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP). Claude installs `dap` if missing (via Homebrew, installer script, or `go install`), then launches a debug session with `dap debug <file>` using auto-detected backend (Python, Go, Node.js/TypeScript, Rust, C/C++). It supports standard breakpoints, conditional breakpoints (e.g. `file:line:condition`), invariant breakpoints, `--stop-on-entry`, `--break-on-exception`, and attaching to remote processes or running PIDs. Navigation commands (`dap step`, `dap step in/out`, `dap continue`, `dap continue --to file:line`) return full context at each stop: current location, source, locals, call stack, and stdout/stderr. `dap eval` evaluates arbitrary expressions against the live process without stepping. The skill emphasizes a hypothesis-driven approach: form a falsifiable hypothesis, set targeted breakpoints, escalate from eval to stepping to conditional breaks, and trace causation up the call stack frame by frame.
use_when: A program crashes or raises an exception whose source isn't obvious from reading code
Output is wrong and you need to observe actual variable values at runtime to find where
Debugging a loop or hot-path bug that requires conditional breakpoints to isolate
Tracing a multi-frame call stack to find where a value first becomes incorrect
not_for: Static analysis or code review (no runtime needed)
Bugs that are obvious from reading the source without running it

name: dispatching-parallel-agents
tagline: Solve multiple independent failures concurrently by dispatching one focused agent per domain

deep_dive: The skill groups failures by independent problem domain (e.g., abort logic, batch completion, race conditions) and dispatches one general-purpose subagent per domain in the same response — issuing multiple Agent tool calls in a single message so they execute concurrently. Each agent receives a self-contained prompt: specific test file/scope, the exact failing test names and error messages, a clear goal, constraints on what not to touch, and an expected output format. After all agents return, the controller reads each summary, checks for conflicting edits to shared files, runs the full test suite to verify fixes integrate cleanly, and spot-checks for systematic errors agents can make. The pattern only applies when failures are genuinely independent; if fixing one might fix others, investigate together first.

It creates todos for every plan item and works through them in order: mark in_progress, follow each bite-sized step exactly, run the specified verifications, mark completed. It stops immediately on any blocker (missing dependency, failing test, unclear instruction) and asks for clarification rather than guessing. After all tasks complete and are verified, it hands off to finishing-a-development-branch, which verifies tests, detects the git environment, and presents structured merge/PR/keep/discard options. name: finishing-a-development-branch
tagline: Gate implementation completion behind test verification, then present merge/PR/keep/discard options

deep_dive: The skill begins by running the full test suite; if tests fail it stops and refuses to present integration options until they pass. Then it detects the git environment by comparing GIT_DIR and GIT_COMMON to distinguish a normal repo, a named-branch worktree (superpowers-created), or a detached HEAD (harness-managed). Based on environment, it presents exactly 4 options (merge locally, push + PR, keep as-is, discard) or 3 for detached HEAD. Each option has precise execution steps: merge locally runs tests on the merged result before any cleanup; push + PR preserves the worktree for PR iteration; discard requires the user to type 'discard' as confirmation. Worktree cleanup only runs for options 1 and 4, and only for worktrees the skill itself created (under .worktrees/ or worktrees/) — harness-owned workspaces are never removed.

name: receiving-code-review
tagline: Evaluate code review feedback with technical rigor — verify before implementing, push back when wrong

deep_dive: The skill enforces a six-step response pattern: read all feedback completely before reacting, restate each requirement in your own words (or ask), verify it against codebase reality, evaluate technical soundness for this specific codebase, respond with technical acknowledgment or reasoned pushback, then implement one item at a time and test each. If any item is unclear, the skill hard-stops before implementing anything — partial understanding leads to wrong implementation. For external reviewer feedback, it applies a skepticism checklist: does this break existing functionality, does the reviewer have full context, are there legacy/compatibility reasons for the current code, does it violate YAGNI? Performative agreement ('You're absolutely right!', 'Great point!') is explicitly forbidden; so is any expression of gratitude. Correct feedback is acknowledged with actions, not words.

Human partner delivers a numbered list of review items

name: requesting-code-review
tagline: Dispatch a focused code-reviewer subagent after each task to catch issues before they compound

deep_dive: The skill works by dispatching a fresh general-purpose subagent using the code-reviewer.md template, giving it precisely crafted context (description of what was built, requirements/plan, BASE_SHA, HEAD_SHA) without exposing the controller's session history. The subagent evaluates the diff and returns findings categorized as Critical, Important, or Minor. The controller then acts: Critical issues are fixed immediately, Important issues are fixed before moving on, Minor issues are logged for later. The reviewer's diff is packaged via the review-package script (which writes it to a file so the reviewer reads one file rather than deriving the diff itself). In subagent-driven-development, this review is mandatory after every task to catch issues before they cascade into later work.

Before merging any feature branch to main

name: subagent-driven-development
tagline: Execute an implementation plan task-by-task using fresh subagents with dual-stage review gates
triggers: A written implementation plan exists and tasks are mostly independent
User says 'implement the plan' or chooses subagent-driven execution after writing-plans
High-quality implementation is needed with spec compliance + code quality gates
Staying in the current session rather than handing off to a new parallel session
deep_dive: The skill reads the plan once, scans for cross-task conflicts, creates todos for all tasks, then enters a tight per-task loop: run task-brief to extract the task text to a file, dispatch a fresh implementer subagent with the brief path + report path + cross-task context (never the full plan), wait for status (DONE / DONE_WITH_CONCERNS / NEEDS_CONTEXT / BLOCKED), generate a review package via review-package script, dispatch a task reviewer subagent with the brief, report, and diff package. The task reviewer must return two verdicts: spec compliance and code quality. Any Critical/Important findings trigger a fix subagent, then re-review. Only when both verdicts pass is the task marked complete in the durable progress ledger (a file under .git/sdd/). After all tasks complete, a final whole-branch reviewer runs on the full branch diff; then finishing-a-development-branch handles merge/PR options. Model selection is explicit per dispatch: cheapest for mechanical 1-2 file tasks, standard for integration, most capable for architecture and final review.

name: systematic-debugging
tagline: Find root cause before fixing anything — four structured phases, no guessing allowed
triggers: Any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior
About to propose a fix before fully understanding the cause
Previous fix attempts didn't work (especially after 2+)
Under time pressure where guessing is tempting
deep_dive: The skill imposes an iron law: no fixes without completing Phase 1 (root cause investigation). Phase 1 requires reading error messages completely, reproducing the issue consistently, checking recent git changes, adding diagnostic instrumentation at each component boundary in multi-layer systems, and tracing the data flow backwards through the call stack to find the original source. Phase 2 finds working examples in the same codebase and identifies every difference between working and broken. Phase 3 forms a single specific hypothesis, tests it with the smallest possible change, and either advances to Phase 4 or forms a new hypothesis — never stacking fixes. Phase 4 creates a failing test case first (via TDD skill), implements the single root-cause fix, and verifies no regressions. If 3+ fixes have failed, the skill mandates stopping to question the architecture with the human partner rather than attempting a fourth fix.
use_when: Any test failure, production bug, or unexpected behavior, no matter how simple it seems
Multiple previous fix attempts have not resolved the issue
Emergency situations where guessing feels faster (systematic is actually faster)
A bug manifests deep in a call stack or across multiple system layers
not_for: Known-cause fixes where root cause is already confirmed (go straight to TDD phase 4)
Performance profiling (different discipline, though phases 1-2 overlap)
Skipping the process because the bug 'seems obvious' — that's a red flag
overlaps_with: debugging-code (systematic-debugging is the methodology; debugging-code is the DAP runtime tool — use both)

name: test-driven-development
tagline: Write the failing test first, watch it fail, then write only enough code to make it pass
triggers: Implementing any new feature, behavior change, or refactor
Fixing a bug (write the failing reproduction test first)
Before writing any production code for a task
Subagent implementers follow this as a required sub-skill
deep_dive: The skill enforces the Red-Green-Refactor cycle as an iron law with no exceptions: write one minimal failing test for one behavior, run it and confirm it fails for the right reason (missing feature, not a typo), write the smallest possible implementation to pass it, confirm all tests pass with pristine output, then refactor without adding behavior. If code was written before the test, the skill requires deleting it completely — not keeping it as 'reference' or adapting it while writing tests. Rationalization tables and red flags are built into the skill to counter every known excuse ('too simple', 'I'll test after', 'deleting is wasteful', 'tests after achieve the same goals'). Tests must use real code rather than mocks where possible; a test that passes immediately means it tests existing behavior and must be fixed before continuing.
use_when: Implementing any new feature or API endpoint
Fixing a bug (write the failing test reproducing it first)
Refactoring existing code that needs test coverage
Subagent implementers working on individual plan tasks
not_for: Throwaway prototypes (ask human partner first)
Generated or configuration files with no testable logic
Skipping because the feature 'seems simple' — that reasoning is explicitly countered by the skill

name: using-git-worktrees
tagline: Detect existing workspace isolation, prefer native tools, fall back to git worktree with safety checks

deep_dive: The skill begins with a mandatory Step 0 detection: compare GIT_DIR and GIT_COMMON to determine if already in a linked worktree (including a submodule guard). If isolation already exists, it skips creation entirely. If not, it asks for user consent before creating anything. Step 1a checks for a native worktree tool (EnterWorktree, /worktree command, --worktree flag) and uses it if available — using git worktree add when a native tool exists is the #1 mistake. Step 1b (git fallback) follows a strict directory-priority order: explicit user preference > existing .worktrees/ or worktrees/ > default .worktrees/, always verifying the directory is .gitignored before creating. Step 2 auto-detects and runs project setup (npm install, pip install, etc.). Step 3 runs the baseline test suite; failing tests trigger a report and a confirmation gate before proceeding.

Executing a plan that requires an isolated workspace

not_for: Quick one-line fixes where isolation overhead isn't worth it (user's call)

name: using-superpowers
tagline: Bootstrap skill discipline: invoke the right skill before any response, even clarifying questions

name: verification-before-completion
tagline: Run the verification command and read its output before making any claim of success or completion
triggers: About to say tests pass, build succeeds, or bug is fixed
About to commit, push, or create a PR

deep_dive: The skill enforces a five-step gate function that must run before any completion claim or expression of satisfaction: identify what command proves the claim, execute it fresh and in full, read the complete output and check the exit code, verify the output actually confirms the claim, and only then make the statement. It explicitly forbids words like 'should', 'probably', 'seems to', and any expression of satisfaction ('Done!', 'Great!', 'Perfect!') before verification has run. For regression tests it requires the full red-green cycle: write the test, confirm it passes, revert the fix to confirm it fails, restore the fix and confirm it passes again. For agent delegation it requires checking the VCS diff to confirm changes actually exist before trusting the agent's report. The skill frames unverified completion claims as dishonesty, not efficiency.

Before committing, creating a PR, or marking a task complete

name: writing-skills
tagline: Apply TDD to process documentation — baseline a failing agent, write the skill, verify compliance
triggers: Creating a new skill or editing an existing one

deep_dive: The skill maps TDD concepts directly to documentation: baseline pressure scenarios are the failing tests, the SKILL.md is the production code, and agent compliance under adversarial pressure is the green pass. The iron law applies: no skill without a failing baseline first — run pressure scenarios without the skill and document exact rationalizations the agent uses. Then write the minimal skill addressing those specific failures (GREEN), test it, and refactor by closing newly discovered loopholes (REFACTOR). The skill includes a 'Match the Form to the Failure' table that prescribes prohibition+rationalization-tables for discipline failures, positive recipe/output contracts for wrong-shaped output, structural required-field templates for omitted elements, and conditional predicates for context-dependent behavior. SDO guidance covers description fields (triggering conditions only, never workflow summaries), keyword coverage, naming conventions, and token efficiency targets. A full creation checklist with RED/GREEN/REFACTOR phases and quality checks must be completed before deployment.

An existing skill isn't working — agents are rationalizing around it

name: frontend-design
tagline: Create distinctive, production-grade frontend interfaces that avoid generic AI aesthetics
triggers: build a web component, page, or frontend app
create a UI with high design quality
design a landing page, dashboard, or web interface
make this look polished and not like generic AI output
deep_dive: The skill guides Claude to produce creative, production-grade frontend code by enforcing a design-first mindset before touching implementation. It starts by identifying the visual language (typography pairing, color palette, spacing system, motion principles) before writing any component code. Output targets real deployed web apps rather than claude.ai artifacts. The skill explicitly prohibits default aesthetic patterns associated with AI-generated UIs: purple/blue gradients, rounded-everything cards, Inter font with gray text, centered hero sections with vague taglines, and glass-morphism overlays. Instead it pushes toward strong typographic hierarchy, intentional whitespace, brand-specific color, and component-level animation. Works with any stack (React, Vue, plain HTML+CSS) and adapts design direction to project context — startup landing page vs. data dashboard vs. documentation site each get different visual treatment.
use_when: Building a web component, page, or full frontend app where design quality matters
